quiz_heme:1.q: Blood is drawn into a tube without anticoagulant, left to stand, and centrifuged. Compared with plasma, the fluid at the arrow lacks which protein?
quiz_heme:1.r: Without anticoagulant the blood clots and the fluid above the clot is serum (p. 371). Plasma minus fibrinogen equals serum (handout p. 434).
quiz_heme:1.alt: Drawing of a centrifuged blood tube with a yellow fluid layer above a dark red layer; an arrow points to the yellow layer.

quiz_heme:12.q: This electron micrograph shows a granulocyte. What is the main protein of the dense crystalline bar at the arrow?
quiz_heme:12.r: Granules with a striped crystalline core identify an eosinophil (p. 1149). The core, or internum, consists primarily of major basic protein, while peroxidase and hydrolytic enzymes sit in the externum around it (p. 395, handout p. 439).
quiz_heme:12.alt: Electron micrograph of a cell whose granules each contain a dark bar; a yellow arrow points to one bar.

quiz_heme:16.q: Up to one third of all the blue-stained elements seen in this normal blood smear are stored in which site?
quiz_heme:16.r: The blue-stained material is a clump of platelets (p. 429). Up to 33% of all blood platelets are stored in the red pulp of the spleen (handout p. 445).
quiz_heme:16.alt: Blood smear with red cells surrounding a cluster of small blue-purple bodies.

quiz_heme:17.q: In this diagram of a platelet, the label of one granule has been replaced by X. Which effect does the lecture attribute to the mediator released from granule X?
quiz_heme:17.r: Granule X is the dense core granule; the alpha granule, lysosome and peroxisome keep their labels. It releases serotonin, which causes vasoconstriction, while endothelial cell mitosis is the effect of platelet-derived growth factor from the alpha granule (p. 421).
quiz_heme:17.alt: Colour diagram of a platelet with labelled organelles; the label of one granule is replaced by the letter X.

quiz_heme:18.q: After a vessel wall is injured, the alpha granules of platelets release platelet-derived growth factor. According to the lecture, what does this factor do?
quiz_heme:18.r: The platelet structure slide links the alpha granule to platelet-derived growth factor and then to endothelial cell mitosis (p. 421). The handout calls this vessel repair (p. 444).

quiz_heme:19.q: This scanning electron micrograph shows platelets seconds after a vessel wall was injured. According to the lecture, what are they sticking to?
quiz_heme:19.r: Key point on the slide: platelets stick immediately to subendothelial collagen (p. 424). The handout adds that this adhesion happens within seconds and is mediated by von Willebrand factor (p. 445).
quiz_heme:19.alt: Scanning electron micrograph of several irregular cells with thin projections lying on a fibrous meshwork.

quiz_heme:3.q: Anticoagulated blood is centrifuged and separates into three layers. According to the handout, about what percentage of the total volume is the top layer?
quiz_heme:3.r: Plasma is the top layer at about 55% of total volume and the buffy coat is about 1% (handout p. 432). The 90% and 10% figures are the water and solutes of plasma (p. 372).

quiz_heme:4.q: In a patient's differential count, the cell type shown makes up 22% of leukocytes. Based on the major function the lecture gives for this cell, which condition is most likely?
quiz_heme:4.r: A bilobed nucleus with large orange-red granules is an eosinophil (p. 394), normally 2 to 4% of leukocytes (p. 364). Its major function is to attack parasites such as helminthic worms (p. 395).
quiz_heme:4.alt: A single nucleated cell among red cells on a stained blood smear.

quiz_heme:6.q: In normal blood, what is the rank order of this leukocyte?
quiz_heme:6.r: A large cell with an indented, horseshoe-shaped nucleus that is not lobed and grey-blue cytoplasm is a monocyte (handout p. 443, p. 1152). At 5% it is third after neutrophils and lymphocytes: N, L, M, E, B (p. 364).
quiz_heme:6.alt: A single large nucleated cell among red cells on a stained blood smear.

quiz_heme:8.q: What is the intravascular lifespan of the leukocyte shown?
quiz_heme:8.r: A multilobed nucleus with fine pale granules is a neutrophil (p. 1147). Its intravascular lifespan is 6 hours and its tissue lifespan 1 to 4 days (p. 391, handout p. 439).
quiz_heme:8.alt: A single nucleated cell among red cells on a stained blood smear.

quiz_heme:9.q: This drawing from an electron micrograph shows a neutrophil. The large dense granule at the arrow holds an enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide into which product?
quiz_heme:9.r: The large dense granules are azurophilic granules, which contain myeloperoxidase (p. 387). Myeloperoxidase converts hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid in oxygen-dependent killing (p. 389).
quiz_heme:9.alt: Electron microscope drawing of a cell with a lobed nucleus and many granules; a yellow arrow points to a large, dark granule.

quiz_heme_b:1.q: Blood collected with an anticoagulant is centrifuged. Which formed elements make up the thin pale layer at the arrow?
quiz_heme_b:1.r: With anticoagulant, spun blood separates into plasma, the buffy coat and erythrocytes; the slide labels the buffy coat as platelets and leukocytes (p. 360).
quiz_heme_b:1.alt: Drawing of a centrifuged blood tube with a yellow upper layer, a thin pale middle layer and a dark red lower layer; an arrow points to the thin middle layer.

quiz_heme_b:10.q: In a patient's differential count, the cell type shown makes up 88% of leukocytes. Based on the major function the lecture gives for this cell, which condition is most likely?
quiz_heme_b:10.r: A multilobed nucleus with fine pale granules is a neutrophil. Its major function is to attack bacteria, and it is normally 60 to 70% of leukocytes, so 88% points to a bacterial infection (p. 364).
quiz_heme_b:10.alt: Single nucleated blood cell with a nucleus in several connected lobes and pale cytoplasm, surrounded by red cells.

quiz_heme_b:11.q: This leukocyte comes from a normal blood smear. What is the small nuclear appendage at the arrow?
quiz_heme_b:11.r: The drumstick on a neutrophil nucleus is the Barr body, the inactive X chromosome (p. 386); the review slide adds that it comes from a female patient (p. 1147).
quiz_heme_b:11.alt: Blood cell with a nucleus of several lobes; an arrow points to a small projection between the lobes.

quiz_heme_b:12.q: This drawing from an electron micrograph shows a neutrophil. Which contents does the lecture give for the small, pale, elongated granule at the arrow?
quiz_heme_b:12.r: The small pale granules are the specific (secondary, salmon pink) granules, which hold proteases and lysozyme. The large dense azurophilic granules hold myeloperoxidase and acid hydrolases (p. 387).
quiz_heme_b:12.alt: Line drawing of a cell with a three-lobed nucleus, several large black granules and many small pale granules; an arrow points to a small pale granule at the left edge.

quiz_heme_b:13.q: In this drawing, leukocytes squeeze between endothelial cells at the arrow and then travel toward the black dot. What are these two processes called, in that order?
quiz_heme_b:13.r: Diapedesis is the migration of leukocytes between endothelial cells into connective tissue (p. 365). The cells then move by chemotaxis toward the chemotactic source, the bacteria releasing chemokines (p. 388).
quiz_heme_b:13.alt: Line drawing of a vessel with cells along its wall, one cell crossing the wall at an arrow, and other cells moving along lines that converge on a black dot.

quiz_heme_b:14.q: According to the lecture, the cell shown limits inflammation by inactivating which mediators?
quiz_heme_b:14.r: The cell is an eosinophil (bilobed nucleus, coarse orange-red granules; faculty practice image p. 428). It attacks parasites and also limits inflammation by inactivating leukotrienes and histamine (p. 398).
quiz_heme_b:14.alt: Blood smear with one nucleated cell that has a two-lobed nucleus and coarse red-orange granules, surrounded by red cells.

quiz_heme_b:15.q: According to the lecture, granules of the cell shown release a chemotactic factor that recruits which cell?
quiz_heme_b:15.r: The cell is a basophil: large dark blue granules partly hide the nucleus (p. 401). Its granules hold heparin, proteases, histamine and eosinophil chemotactic factor, and one of its functions is to recruit eosinophils (p. 402, p. 397).
quiz_heme_b:15.alt: Blood smear with one nucleated cell filled with large dark purple granules, surrounded by red cells.

quiz_heme_b:16.q: According to the lecture's differential count slide, what is the major function of the cell shown?
quiz_heme_b:16.r: A round condensed nucleus with only a thin rim of cytoplasm is a lymphocyte (p. 409). Lymphocytes mediate humoral and cellular immunity (p. 364).
quiz_heme_b:16.alt: Single small blood cell with a round dark nucleus that nearly fills it, surrounded by red cells.

quiz_heme_b:17.q: Which of the following develops from the cell shown after it leaves the blood?
quiz_heme_b:17.r: The large cell with an indented nucleus and no specific granules is a monocyte (p. 415). Monocytes become tissue macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system, such as the Kupffer cell of the liver (p. 417); plasma cells derive from B lymphocytes (p. 409).
quiz_heme_b:17.alt: Blood smear with one large nucleated cell that has an indented nucleus and pale cytoplasm, surrounded by red cells and small dark fragments.

quiz_heme_b:18.q: According to the lecture, how long does the small dark body at the arrow remain in the circulation?
quiz_heme_b:18.r: The small body between the erythrocytes is a platelet (p. 420), and the platelet structure slide gives 10 days in circulation (p. 421). Six hours and 1 to 4 days belong to neutrophils (p. 391), 120 days to erythrocytes (p. 383).
quiz_heme_b:18.alt: Blood smear at high magnification with large red cells; an arrow points to a small dark purple body between them.

quiz_heme_b:19.q: In this scheme of hemostasis from the lecture, two outcomes have been replaced by X and Y. What belongs at X?
quiz_heme_b:19.r: Platelet adhesion, activation and aggregation give the primary hemostatic plug. Fibrin from the clotting cascade then converts it into the definitive hemostatic plug, which is Y (p. 422).
quiz_heme_b:19.alt: Flow chart on a black background: vascular injury leads to three boxes for vasoconstriction, platelets and the clotting cascade; two outcome labels are replaced by the letters X and Y.

quiz_heme_b:2.q: This drawing shows three spun hematocrit tubes beside a percentage scale. The tube at the arrow came from a patient with a diseased kidney; which cause listed in the lecture best explains the result?
quiz_heme_b:2.r: The packed cell column is far below normal, the tube the slide labels anemia (p. 359). Low erythropoietin from a diseased kidney is the slide's example of insufficient production of RBCs (p. 382).
quiz_heme_b:2.alt: Line drawing of three narrow tubes with dark columns of different heights next to a scale from 0 to 100; an arrow points to the middle tube.

quiz_heme_b:20.q: A boy with hemophilia A cuts his finger. Based on the lecture's account of hemostasis, which step fails?
quiz_heme_b:20.r: Hemophilia A is absence of Factor VIII. Von Willebrand factor binds Factor VIII from plasma to form fibrin, so clot formation with fibrin fails while vasoconstriction and platelet aggregation still occur (p. 423).

quiz_heme_b:3.q: Antibodies circulate in the plasma. According to the lecture, to which plasma protein fraction do they belong, and what share of plasma protein is that fraction?
quiz_heme_b:3.r: Globulins (35%) include the immunoglobulins (antibodies) and the transport globulins; albumin is 60% and fibrinogen 4% (p. 373).

quiz_heme_b:4.q: A man's blood count shows 15,000 leukocytes per mm3 with 65% neutrophils, hematocrit 45%, hemoglobin 15 g/dL and 300,000 platelets per mm3. Which value lies outside the normal range given in the lecture?
quiz_heme_b:4.r: Normal leukocytes are 4,500 to 11,000 per mm3. Neutrophils 60 to 70%, hematocrit 40 to 54% and hemoglobin 13.8 to 17.2 g/dL for men, and platelets 150,000 to 450,000 per mm3 are all met here (p. 364).

quiz_heme_b:5.q: A complete blood count report lists the indices below. Which one does the lecture say measures inflammation?
quiz_heme_b:5.r: ESR is the erythrocyte sedimentation rate and measures inflammation. MCV, MCHC and RDW describe red cell volume, hemoglobin concentration and size distribution, and MPV is mean platelet volume (p. 425).

quiz_heme_b:6.q: The cells at the yellow arrows are immature forms of the pale cells around them. According to the lecture, what do they still contain?
quiz_heme_b:6.r: Reticulocytes show remnants of RNA and have a larger diameter than mature erythrocytes; both lack a nucleus (review slide p. 1145).
quiz_heme_b:6.alt: Blood smear with pale round cells; two cells marked by yellow arrows contain dark blue speckles.

quiz_heme_b:7.q: This diagram shows the erythrocyte membrane and its skeleton. What does the blue channel at the arrow carry across the membrane?
o: Oxygen in exchange for carbon dioxide
quiz_heme_b:7.r: The blue channel is the anion transporter, band 3. It lets bicarbonate cross the membrane in exchange for chloride, which facilitates release of CO2 in the lung (p. 379).
quiz_heme_b:7.alt: Diagram of a lipid bilayer with two green transmembrane proteins, a blue channel in the centre marked by an arrow, and a meshwork of filaments underneath.

quiz_heme_b:8.q: Which lettered cell in this normal blood smear has granules that contain a neurotoxin?
quiz_heme_b:8.r: Cell D is the eosinophil (bilobed nucleus, orange-pink granules; labelled on p. 365). The crystalline internum of its granules holds major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein and neurotoxin (p. 395; faculty practice question p. 426).
quiz_heme_b:8.alt: Blood smear with many red cells and five nucleated cells marked with the letters A to E.

quiz_heme_b:9.q: In normal blood, the cell at the blue arrow will complete its differentiation. About what share of circulating leukocytes does its mature form make up?
quiz_heme_b:9.r: The cell with the unsegmented, band-shaped nucleus is a band (immature) neutrophil and matures into a neutrophil (faculty practice question p. 427). Neutrophils are 60 to 70% of leukocytes (p. 364).
quiz_heme_b:9.alt: Blood smear with red cells and several nucleated cells; a blue arrow points to one nucleated cell with a curved nucleus.

brief:
Hematology High-Yield Tables (Exam 3)

Hematology (Djakiew) was 26/36 (72%) on your September quiz; platelets and hemostasis (2/6) and handout-only questions (4/11) were weakest. Page numbers are pages of the combined PDF: slides pp. 356 to 431, handout pp. 432 to 445, blood-cell slides of his review lecture pp. 1145 to 1152 and 1171. Everything is from those pages unless labeled (outside the slides). A fact marked (handout) appears only in the handout.

1. Blood composition and plasma proteins (LO 1)

Blood is a connective tissue made of formed elements suspended in plasma, and a spun tube shows the proportions (pp. 358, 360, 361, 432).

Blood transports (p. 358)
Oxygen and other nutrients
Waste products, such as carbon dioxide (handout)
Hormones
Heat
Cells
Part of blood Made of Page
Formed elements Red blood cells (RBC, erythrocytes), white blood cells (WBC, leukocytes), platelets (from megakaryocytes) 361
Plasma Water 90%, solutes 10% 372
Solutes Proteins, small organics, inorganics 372, 373
Layer after spinning with anticoagulant Share of volume Contains Page
Plasma (top) About 55% (handout) Protein-rich liquid 360, 432
Buffy coat (thin middle) About 1% (handout) Leukocytes and platelets 360, 432
Erythrocytes (bottom) Male 40 to 50%, female 35 to 45% (handout) Packed red cells; this is the hematocrit 360, 432
Tube Top fluid Bottom Rule Page
With anticoagulant Plasma Buffy coat, then erythrocytes Plasma still holds fibrinogen 371
Without anticoagulant Serum Clot Plasma minus fibrinogen = serum (handout) 371, 434
Clinical test What it is Page
Hematocrit (packed cell volume) Volume of blood occupied by erythrocytes, as a % or a fraction (handout) 359, 432
Low hematocrit tube Anemia 359
High hematocrit tube Polycythemia 359
Differential count Number of each type of leukocyte (section 2) 362, 432
Normal value Slide (p. 364) Handout Fig 5 (p. 435) or text (p. 432)
Leukocytes 4,500 to 11,000/mm3 6,000 to 9,000/mm3
Hematocrit Women 36 to 48%, men 40 to 54% Female 35 to 45%, male 40 to 50%
Hemoglobin Women 12.1 to 15.1 g/dL, men 13.8 to 17.2 g/dL Not given
Platelets 150,000 to 450,000/mm3 200,000 to 400,000/mm3
Red cells Not given 4 to 5 million/mm3 (handout)

The slide and the handout give different normal ranges for leukocytes, hematocrit and platelets. Answer his handout numbers unless the question quotes the slide's ranges.

Plasma protein Share Job Extra Page
Albumin 60% on the slide; 50 to 60% in the handout Maintains osmotic pressure; transports bilirubin Made by the liver; has a hydrophobic pocket that carries substances; tallest peak on electrophoresis, Fig 7 (handout) 373, 434, 435
Globulins: alpha, beta, gamma 35% Immunoglobulins (antibodies); transport globulins bind small ions, hormones and other compounds Immunoglobulin is made by plasma cells (handout) 372, 373, 434
Fibrinogen 4% on the slide; 7% in the handout Forms blood clots Precursor of fibrin; absent from serum (handout) 373, 434
Complement Not given Immune response and inflammation (handout) 434
Lipoproteins Not given Lipid transport (handout) 434

Albumin and fibrinogen percentages differ between slide and handout. Answer the handout (albumin 50 to 60%, fibrinogen 7%) unless the question uses the slide's set of 60%, 35% and 4%.

Plasma proteins are classified by electrophoresis and by solubility in water (handout, p. 434).

Other solutes Examples Page
Small organics Lipids (fatty acids, cholesterol, glycerides), carbohydrates (mainly glucose), amino acids, organic wastes (urea, creatinine, bilirubin) 373
Other organics in the handout Organic acids, vitamins, hormones (handout) 434
Inorganics Electrolytes: sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, chloride, bicarbonate, phosphate, sulfate 373
Inorganics in the handout Blood gases (handout) 434
Lab report term (p. 425) Meaning
MCV Mean corpuscular (red cell) volume
MCH Mean corpuscular hemoglobin
MCHC Mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
RDW Red blood cell distribution: deviation from the normal distribution
MPV Mean platelet volume
ESR Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; measures inflammation

2. The differential count as a diagnostic (LO 2)

A differential count is the number of each type of leukocyte, given as an absolute number per unit volume or as a % of the white cell count (handout, p. 432).

Smear and stain Detail Page
Stain Romanovsky-type, such as Wright's or Giemsa (names are handout) 362, 432
Solvent Alcohol solution that fixes and stains at the same time (handout) 432
Basophilic Blue 362
Azurophilic Purple 362
Eosinophilic Orange 362
Neutrophilic Pink; salmon pink in the handout 362, 432
Rank Cell Slide % Handout Fig 5 % Major function on the slide A high count points to
1 Neutrophil 60 to 70% 55 to 60% Attack bacteria Bacterial infection; acute inflammation
2 Lymphocyte 28% 30 to 35% Mediate humoral and cellular immunity An immune response to antigen
3 Monocyte 5% 3 to 7% Become phagocytic macrophages Demand for macrophages
4 Eosinophil 2 to 4% 2 to 5% Attack parasites Parasites such as helminthic worms; allergic inflammation
5 Basophil 0.5% 0 to 1% Mediate inflammation Immediate hypersensitivity, such as asthma

Pages for that table: 364, 385, 395, 404, 435, 438, 441, 443. The slides give each cell's job, not a list of causes of a high count; the last column is that job read backwards, which is what LO 2 asks you to do.

The percentages differ between the slides and handout Fig 5. Answer the slide numbers here, because they are repeated on six slides and his own handout text also says neutrophils are 60 to 70% (p. 439); the rank order is the same in both.

Mnemonic for rank order: Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas (p. 364).

Group Members Specific granules Nucleus Page
Granulocytes Neutrophil, eosinophil, basophil Yes Segmented 366, 432
Agranulocytes ("mononuclear cells") Lymphocyte, monocyte No, but they do have non-specific (azurophilic) granules (handout) Spherical or slightly indented (handout) 368, 432
Reading a count Rule Page
Band neutrophil Immature neutrophil whose nucleus has not finished segmenting; completes differentiation into a neutrophil 365, 427, 438
What a blood sample measures Only the circulating neutrophil pool, not the marginated pool, Fig 15 (handout) 442
Automated analysis More than 500 samples each day at the hospital; cells sorted by fluorescence and side scatter 363
Property shared by leukocytes Detail Page
Diapedesis Migration of leukocytes between endothelial cells into connective tissue 365
Where and when All leukocytes do it, mostly at capillaries and venules; greatly increased in inflammation by cytokines (handout) 434
Who stays inside vessels Erythrocytes and platelets (handout) 434
Phagocytosis Granulocytes and monocytes (handout) 434
Surface receptors For cytokines (chemotactic factors) and for opsonization, which enhances phagocytosis (handout) 434

3. Every blood cell in one table (LO 3)

Know each cell by its nucleus and granules first, then attach its numbers and job (pp. 375 to 421, 436 to 445, 1145 to 1152).

Cell Size Nucleus Granules and contents Lifespan Function Recognise it by
Erythrocyte 8 µm wide, 2 µm thick (handout) None None; packed with hemoglobin 120 days Exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide Pink disc with a pale centre and no nucleus; most plentiful cell
Reticulocyte Larger than a mature red cell None Remnants of RNA RNA lasts 1 to 2 days (handout) New red cell finishing hemoglobin synthesis (handout) Blue network with a supravital stain; about 1% of red cells (handout)
Neutrophil Not given 2 to 5 lobes (handout) Specific (salmon pink) and azurophilic (purple) 6 hours in blood; 1 to 4 days in tissue Phagocytose and kill bacteria; form pus Multilobed nucleus, fine pale granules
Eosinophil Not given Bilobed (handout) Large, spherical; externum and crystalline internum Not given Attack parasites; limit inflammation Two lobes plus large orange-red granules
Basophil Not given 2 to 3 lobes, less segmented (handout) Large basophilic granules: histamine, heparin, proteases, eosinophil chemotactic factor Not given Inflammation; recruit eosinophils Dark granules that partly hide the nucleus
Lymphocyte Small 8 to 9 µm; a few up to 16 µm (handout) Round to oval, condensed A few azurophilic granules (handout) Some survive many years (handout) Humoral and cellular immunity Nucleus fills most of the cell; thin rim of blue cytoplasm
Monocyte Largest leukocyte (handout) Eccentric, indented or horseshoe, not lobed (handout) A few azurophilic granules and vacuoles (handout) 40 hours in blood (handout); months in tissue Become phagocytic macrophages Big cell, indented nucleus, grey-blue cytoplasm
Platelet 2 to 3 µm (handout) None Alpha, dense and lambda granules 10 days Hemostasis and vascular repair Tiny purple fragments, far smaller than any cell; clump on smears

Pages by row: erythrocyte 375, 381, 383, 436, 438; reticulocyte 436, 1145; neutrophil 386, 387, 391, 438, 439, 1147; eosinophil 394, 395, 398, 439, 441, 1148; basophil 401, 402, 441, 443, 1150; lymphocyte 407, 409, 443, 1151; monocyte 415, 417, 443, 444, 1152; platelet 420, 421, 444, 445, 1145. The "recognise it by" wording describes his images and is mine.

The slide figure gives the monocyte a blood half-time of 1 to 3 days (p. 417), while the handout says circulating lifespan is 40 hours (p. 444). Answer 40 hours unless the question quotes the figure.

Red cell fact Detail Page
Shape Biconcave disc; more surface area than a sphere (handout) 436
Membrane strength Withstands shear at heart valves; holds an osmotic pressure 5 times that of serum (handout) 436
Membrane plasticity Lets the cell pass a 3 to 4 µm capillary; minimizes blood viscosity (handout) 436
Submembrane skeleton Spectrin, actin and other proteins; keeps the biconcave shape (handout) 436
Ankyrin Anchors spectrin to band 3 379
Band 3 Anion transporter: bicarbonate out for chloride in; helps release carbon dioxide in the lung 379
Glycophorin and band 3 The two major transmembrane proteins exposed on the outer surface 379
Membrane carbohydrate Sets the ABO blood type; negative charge helps prevent agglutination (handout) 380, 436
What it lacks Nucleus, ribosomes, mitochondria; cannot make protein, including hemoglobin (handout) 383, 438
Energy Anaerobic glycolysis makes the ATP for membrane integrity and hemoglobin function (handout) 438
Key point Integrity depends on the cell membrane, hemoglobin and metabolic enzymes 378
Why 120 days No nucleus, so damaged proteins cannot be repaired or replaced 383
Removal More than 90% extravascular: spleen, liver, bone marrow; less than 10% intravascular 383
Fate of hemoglobin Macrophages break it into iron and bilirubin (handout) 438
Time in marrow 7 to 8 days of production and release 383
ABO antigen (p. 380) Sugar added to the O antigen
O None
A N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)
B Galactose
Hemoglobin (Hb) fact Detail Page
Heme Four heme groups per molecule; iron is the oxygen-binding site (handout) 436
Globin Tetramer of two pairs of chains (handout) 436
Adult mix HbA 97%, HbA2 2 to 3%, fetal HbF under 1% (handout) 436
Sickle cell anemia Point mutation, glutamic acid to valine; sickled, inflexible cells are removed by the spleen 381
Anemia (low hemoglobin concentration), p. 382 Example
Loss of blood Hemorrhage
Insufficient production of red cells Low erythropoietin from a diseased kidney
Red cells with insufficient hemoglobin Iron deficiency
Accelerated red cell destruction Sickle cells
Neutrophil granule Stain and size Contents on the slide Added by the handout Page
Specific (secondary) Salmon pink; small, close to the limit of resolution; the majority Proteases and lysozyme Lactoferrin, NADPH oxidase, lysozyme, vitamin B12-binding protein, alkaline phosphatase; peroxidase negative 387, 438
Azurophilic (non-specific, primary lysosomes) Purple; large and dense; 10 to 20% of granules (handout) Myeloperoxidase and acid hydrolases Defensins, bacterial permeability increasing protein, proteolytic enzymes; peroxidase positive; present in all leukocytes 387, 438

The slide puts proteases in the specific granules, while the handout puts proteolytic enzymes in the azurophilic granules. Answer the handout; lysozyme (specific) and myeloperoxidase (azurophilic) are safe in both.

Neutrophil fact Detail Page
Other name Polymorphonuclear leukocyte ("poly") 386
Drumstick Barr body, the inactive X chromosome; about 3% of neutrophils in women (handout) 386, 438
Hypersegmented More than 5 lobes (handout) 438
Circulating pool 50%, suspended in blood (handout) 439
Marginated pool 50%, reversibly stuck to endothelium, especially in the lung (handout) 439
Marrow reserve 10 times the number in blood (handout) 439
Metabolism Few mitochondria, abundant glycogen; works without oxygen (handout) 439
Side effect Reactive oxygen species may damage DNA and cause cancer 390
Step to the bacteria What happens Page
1. Margination: rolling Selectins (handout) 438, 440
2. Margination: sticking, then transmigration Integrins (handout) 438, 440
3. Diapedesis Cell squeezes between endothelial cells, after about 6 hours in the blood 388, 391
4. Chemotaxis Follows chemokines secreted by resident tissue cells in the inflamed area 388, 439
5. Recognition and phagocytosis Through receptors; greatly enhanced by opsonization with antibody or complement (handout) 389, 439
6. Oxygen-dependent killing Superoxide and hydrogen peroxide; myeloperoxidase turns hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid 389
7. Oxygen-independent killing Lysosomes; a proton pump acidifies the phagosome and both granule types empty into it (handout) 389, 439
8. End Dead neutrophils form pus; tissue life 1 to 4 days 391, 439
Eosinophil granule part Contents Page
Externum (less dense matrix) Peroxidase, hydrolytic enzymes 395, 439
Internum (crystalline core) Major basic protein, eosinophil cationic protein, neurotoxin 395, 441
Major basic protein Main part of the core; anti-parasitic; gives the granule its eosinophilia; most abundant granule protein (handout) 439
Eosinophil cationic protein Most potent tissue-damaging protein of the cell (handout) 441
Eosinophil fact Detail Page
Main job Attacks parasites, such as helminthic worms 395, 396
Second job Limits inflammation by inactivating leukotrienes and histamine 398
Also Phagocytoses antigen-antibody complexes (handout) 441
What calls it Eosinophil chemotactic factor from basophils and mast cells 397, 441
Where it lives Tissues with an epithelial surface to the outside: respiratory, gastrointestinal, lower genitourinary tracts (handout) 441
Under the electron microscope Granules show striped crystals 1149
Basophil mediator When Effect Page
Histamine Preformed in granules Raises vascular permeability; contracts smooth muscle in the lungs (handout) 402, 441
Heparin Preformed Anticoagulant; gives the granules their basophilia (handout) 402, 441
Proteases Preformed 402, 441
Eosinophil chemotactic factor Preformed Recruits eosinophils 402, 441
Leukotrienes Made only after activation, not stored (handout) 441
Basophil fact Detail Page
Trigger Antigen bridges immunoglobulin E (IgE) held on surface receptors 403, 441
Timing Granule mediators in 1 to 5 minutes, lipid mediators in 5 to 30 minutes, cytokines in minutes to hours 403
Effects in asthma Eosinophil chemoattraction, edema from leaky vessels, bronchoconstriction, mucus hypersecretion 404
Disease Immediate hypersensitivity 404, 443
Compared with a mast cell Similar, not identical; mast cells have round or oval nuclei; basophil granules are fewer but larger (handout) 441
Frequency Least common leukocyte 443
Lymphocyte fact Detail Page
Small versus large Most are small; the larger ones are activated cells responding to antigen (handout) 443
Unlike other leukocytes Re-enter the blood through lymphatics, can still divide, some live for years (handout) 443
T cells Cell-mediated immunity 411
B cells Humoral immunity; become plasma cells 409, 411
Plasma cell Eccentric nucleus; abundant cytoplasm with Golgi and rough endoplasmic reticulum 409
Natural killer cell Granular cytoplasm 409

5. The steps of hemostasis in order (LO 4)

Hemostasis keeps blood fluid yet confined within the vessels, and after injury it runs as six steps (handout, p. 445).

Step Name What happens Result
1 Reflex vasoconstriction The injured vessel narrows Reduced blood loss
2 Platelet adhesion Within seconds platelets stick to subendothelial collagen, through vWF
3 Contact activation and release Adherent platelets release mediators that enhance hemostasis (handout) Hemostasis enhanced
4 Platelet aggregation Platelets stick to each other through fibrinogen (handout) Primary platelet plug: primary hemostasis
5 Fibrin formation The coagulation cascade makes thrombin, which converts soluble fibrinogen to insoluble fibrin, over hours (handout) Definitive plug: secondary hemostasis
6 Clot retraction The clot condenses, using platelet actin, myosin and ATP (handout) Condensed clot
